The species is monoecious, with male and female cones occurring on the same plant. Male cones are small, terminal, and cylindrical, while female cones are more rounded and produce winged seeds that are dispersed by wind. Pollination occurs during the warmer months, with cones maturing over an extended period. 

Diselma archeri is endemic to Tasmania, where it occupies a restricted range of high-altitude habitats, typically above 800 metres. It thrives in moist, well-drained soils within subalpine woodland and rainforest communities, often forming dense thickets in sheltered gullies and on rocky slopes. The species is highly sensitive to fire and regeneration is slow following disturbance. Populations are considered secure within protected areas, though climate change and increased fire frequency pose potential long-term threats to its alpine and subalpine habitat.

pair.human_continuation:
The square leaf arrangement is similar to that of Microcachrys tetragona (Podocarpaceae) (creeping pine) and the two species can easily be confused. However, M. tetragona lives up to its name and grows low to the ground, spreading out with only occasional erect branches. Another species which can be confused with Diselma is Phaerosphaera hookeriana (previously known as Microstrobos niphophilus ) which is in the family Podocarpaceae. Both these species have a similar growth habit and distribution, however, the opposite pairs of leaves on D. archeri again make it distinguishable from the other species. 
Bark is rough and scaly and often weathered revealing a reddish-brown inner bark.
Being a gymnosperm no flowers are produced, instead seed development occurs on the surface of the scale-like leaves which are modified to form cones (see image).
pair.prefix:
Appearance and ecology 
 
Diselma archeri is a compact, prostrate shrub which commonly reaches 1–4 m in height but has been recorded to reach greater heights in subalpine rainforest zones. The foliage has a grey-green appearance with branchlets curving downward at their tips. Branches are short, ridged and very numerous. Branchlet foliage appears square in cross-section and scale-like leaves (2–3 mm) are overlapping and arranged in opposite decussate pairs which are pressed close to the stem.
